title: Role taking and knowledge building in a blended university course
authors: Donatella Cesareni & Stefano Cacciamani & Nobuko Fujita
summary_haiku: Assigning scripted roles aligned with knowledge-building principles significantly enhances student participation in blended university courses. Two studies examined 143 students across three modules, comparing role-takers with non-role-takers using quantitative participation metrics and qualitative content analysis. Results demonstrated that role-takers demonstrated higher reading and writing activity, varied their conversational functions more broadly, and engaged in greater synthesis and metacognitive reflection, supporting collective cognitive responsibility for knowledge advancement.

title: Tracing the change in discourse in a collaborative dynamic geometry environment: From visual to more mathematical
authors: Diler Oner
summary_haiku: This case study examined three middle-school students' mathematical discourse development while solving geometry construction problems in the Virtual Math Teams collaborative environment. Using Sfard's commognitive framework, the researcher traced changes in students' word usage, visual mediators, and problem-solving routines across six episodes. The team progressively shifted from visual, perception-based approaches to more formal mathematical discourse emphasizing geometric dependencies, demonstrating that well-designed collaborative virtual learning environments can support significant mathematical development comparable to expert instruction.

title: Exploring the relationship between resistance and perspectival understanding in computer-mediated discussions
authors: SoonAh Lee & Kwangok Song
summary_haiku: This discourse analytic study examined how graduate students expressed resistance while negotiating ideas in computer-mediated discussions. Findings revealed that resistance expressions frequently accompanied perspectival understanding as students elaborated on course readings and peer ideas. Resistance functioned as a constructive discourse tool, facilitating both individual and collaborative knowledge construction. The study demonstrates resistance's integral role in developing sophisticated perspectives within online classroom discussions.

title: Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students’ conceptual understanding
authors: Anniken Furberg
summary_haiku: This intervention study examined teacher support in computer-supported collaborative lab work, analyzing 122 student help requests during a genetics experiment. Findings reveal that 45.1% of requests concerned conceptual issues and 28.7% addressed procedural challenges. Detailed interaction analyses show students struggled linking lab procedures to underlying scientific principles, requiring substantial teacher support through elicitation, explanation, and conceptual guidance to bridge this gap.

title: Group emotions: the social and cognitive functions of emotions in argumentation
authors: Claire Polo & Kristine Lund & Christian Plantin & Gerald P. Niccolai
summary_haiku: Emotions serve dual functions in group argumentation: socially, they signal recognition and engagement in specific talk types (cumulative, disputational, exploratory); cognitively, they frame discourse objects through schematization. Analysis of student debates reveals low-intensity emotional framing correlates with cumulative talk, while high-intensity framing correlates with disputational talk, suggesting optimal emotional engagement supports higher-quality collaborative reasoning.

title: Cultural ways of constructing knowledge: the role of identities in online group discussions
authors: Murat Oztok
summary_haiku: This study explores how students utilize multiple identification categories—such as gender, profession, ethnicity, and group affinity—during online group discussions to construct knowledge collaboratively. Through case analysis of asynchronous threaded discussions in a graduate education course, the research demonstrates that individuals flexibly enact different identities at various knowledge-construction phases, using personal experiences to negotiate meaning and advance collective understanding. The findings reveal that identification plays a central role in mediating between personal cognition and social learning processes.

title: Quantitative approach to collaborative learning: performance prediction, individual assessment, and group composition
authors: Ling Cen & Dymitr Ruta & Leigh Powell & Benjamin Hirsch & Jason Ng
summary_haiku: This study applies machine learning techniques to predict group performance in computer-supported collaborative learning using interaction data from 122 students across three assignments. The research develops normalized features capturing collaboration patterns and proposes a comparative model to assess individual student contributions within groups. Results demonstrate 79% classification accuracy and reveal that heterogeneous groups with mixed genders and diverse skill levels achieve significantly greater collaborative synergy than homogeneous groups.

title: The symmetry of partner modelling
authors: Pierre Dillenbourg & Mirweis Sangin & Nicolas Nova
summary_haiku: This study examines whether collaborative partners' mutual modeling accuracy—their ability to understand each other's knowledge, intentions, and emotions—depends on individual cognitive skills or interaction quality. Analyzing five experiments across different collaborative tasks, the researchers found that partners' modeling accuracy was significantly correlated in four studies, suggesting interaction quality matters more than individual abilities. However, correlations remained moderate, indicating both factors contribute to mutual understanding in collaborative learning.

title: You like it, you learn it: affectivity and learning in competitive social role play gaming
authors: Cyril Brom & Michaela Slussareff & Tereza Selmbacherova
summary_haiku: This study examined whether positive affect mediates learning gains in game-based education using a between-subjects design with 325 high school and college students. Participants learned about EU policy through a debate-based method delivered via computer game, non-computer game, or traditional workshop. Both game conditions induced higher positive affect and flow, and participants learned more with games. Positive affect—but not flow—mediated the relationship between instructional medium and learning outcomes, suggesting that affective engagement is crucial for game-based learning effectiveness.

title: Socially shared regulation of learning in CSCL: understanding and prompting individual- and group-level shared regulatory activities
authors: Sanna Jarvela & Paul A. Kirschner & Allyson Hadwin & Hanna Jarvenoja & Jonna Malmberg & Mariel Miller & Jari Laru
summary_haiku: This review examines socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) in computer-supported collaborative learning. The authors identify gaps in existing CSCL support tools, which focus on knowledge construction and social awareness but neglect regulatory processes. They present conceptual frameworks distinguishing self-regulated, co-regulated, and socially shared regulation, then describe multiple tools (AIRE, SEST, planning tools, VCRI+SSRL, S-REG) designed to prompt metacognitive awareness and support individual and group-level regulation of cognition, motivation, and emotion during collaborative tasks.

title: Contribution to a theory of CSCL scripts: taking into account the appropriation of scripts by learners
authors: Pierre Tchounikine
summary_haiku: Tchounikine argues that understanding CSCL script enactment requires examining learner appropriation—how learners perceive, understand, and make scripts their own—rather than assuming direct script implementation. Through theoretical analysis, he demonstrates that appropriation involves complex cognitive processes influenced by technology use, institutional contexts, and domain-specific factors. The paper proposes that appropriation and implementation are intertwined processes requiring holistic analysis, extending the Script Theory of Guidance framework.

title: Appropriation from a script theory of guidance perspective: a response to Pierre Tchounikine
authors: Karsten Stegmann & Ingo Kollar & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This response clarifies how Script Theory of Guidance (SToG) addresses learner appropriation of collaboration scripts. The authors argue SToG inherently concerns appropriation through three mechanisms: learners' goals influence internal script configuration, perceived situational characteristics shape script interpretation, and appropriation involves perception, interpretation, and implementation steps. They propose that internalization follows successful appropriation, and acknowledge that institutional and domain-specific factors merit stronger theoretical integration within SToG's framework.

title: Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement
authors: Yuqin Yang & Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Wen Tian
summary_haiku: Students with low academic achievement engaged in sustained knowledge-building discourse when supported by reflective assessment using the Knowledge Connections Analyzer tool. Analysis of 20 Grade 11 visual arts students' online discussions revealed they generated theories, built on peers' ideas, and synthesized concepts. Reflective assessment helped students focus on knowledge-building goals including community collaboration, idea improvement, and synthesis, demonstrating that low-achieving students can successfully participate in higher-order collaborative inquiry.

title: Improving collaborative learning in the classroom: Text mining based grouping and representing
authors: Daniel Bodemer & Melanie Erkens & H. Ulrich Hoppe
summary_haiku: This study developed and tested the Grouping and Representing Tool (GRT), which uses text mining to automatically form heterogeneous learning groups and visualize students' knowledge. Comparing Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Vector Space Models, researchers found LDA superior for visualizing cognitive information while Euclidean distance-based clustering better identified text differences for grouping. An experimental evaluation with 54 high school students showed GRT-supported dyads achieved twice the knowledge gains compared to unsupported groups, demonstrating text mining's effectiveness for supporting collaborative learning.

title: What happens when you push the button? Analyzing the functional dynamics of concept development in computer supported science inquiry
authors: Hans Christian Arnseth & Ingeborg Krange
summary_haiku: This study examines how high school students develop scientific concepts through computer-supported collaborative inquiry into energy transformation. Using video ethnography, researchers analyzed students' interactions with material and digital tools while learning to explain how a heat pump works. Results demonstrate that students progressively developed sophisticated use of science concepts as explanatory tools through a functional system comprising teacher guidance, material artifacts, and digital models. Teacher practices—including eliciting understanding, providing strategic hints, and modeling coherent concept use—were crucial for supporting students' conceptual development across multiple representations.

title: Conversational agents for academically productive talk: a comparison of directed and undirected agent interventions
authors: Stergios Tegos & Stavros Demetriadis & Pantelis M. Papadopoulos & Armin Weinberger
summary_haiku: This study compared directed versus undirected conversational agent interventions promoting academically productive talk in 96 computer science students working in dyads. Using a pre-test/post-test experimental design with discourse analysis, results showed directed interventions—addressing individual students—significantly enhanced individual domain knowledge and explicit reasoning compared to undirected interventions addressing both peers. Explicit reasoning mediated the agent's effect on dyad performance, with directed methods proving more effective at stimulating productive discourse.

title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
authors: Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Ella L. F. Fu
summary_haiku: This study developed a classification of nine discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions using qualitative coding and narrative analysis of Knowledge Forum databases across three classes. The patterns distinguished three modes of discourse—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building—revealing how students engage in collaborative interactions. Knowledge-sharing discourse predominated, while knowledge-building discourse was rare, suggesting that supporting productive discourse requires explicit pedagogical guidance aligned with learning principles.

title: This is the size of one meter: Children’s bodily-material collaboration
authors: Jacob Davidsen & Thomas Ryberg
summary_haiku: Two nine-year-old children collaborating around a touchscreen demonstrate that bodily-material resources—gestures, movements, and touch—function as primary vehicles for learning about scale and measurement, not merely supplementary to language. Through detailed video analysis, the study reveals children use bodies communicatively to illustrate understanding, cognitively as auxiliary tools scaffolding knowledge, and physically to shepherd each other's learning in the space between themselves and the screen.

title: DCLM framework: understanding collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments
authors: Matthew Berland & Leilah Lyons & Mike Tissenbaum
summary_haiku: This paper introduces the Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM) framework for analyzing collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments where participants pursue divergent goals. Extending the existing Collaborative Learning Mechanisms framework, DCLM adds six mechanisms including boundary spanning actions and perception, goal adaptation, and modeling. Analysis of the Oztoc museum exhibit demonstrates that participants with non-aligned goals can productively collaborate, providing insights unavailable in shared-goal activities.

title: A more reflective form of joint problem solving
authors: Richard Alterman & Kendall Harsch
summary_haiku: This study examines asynchronous online collaboration among university students completing wiki and blog-based writing assignments. Through qualitative analysis of over 7,000 lines of chat transcripts, the research identifies how participants create "venues"—virtual spaces anchoring joint problem-solving across different times and places. The findings reveal a shift toward more reflective, piecemeal collaboration compared to face-to-face interaction, with participants strategically selecting problems for joint attention while leveraging secondary participation through reading and reflection.

title: Group practices: a new way of viewing CSCL
authors: Gerry Stahl
summary_haiku: Stahl proposes analyzing group practices—observable, routinized behaviors enacted by small collaborative teams—as central to understanding computer-supported collaborative learning. Using design-based research with the Virtual Math Teams project, he demonstrates that groups adopt practices through breakdowns and negotiation, mediating between individual cognition and cultural knowledge. This approach provides systematic methodology for CSCL design, theory, and analysis beyond traditional pre/post comparisons.

title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
authors: Oskar Lindwall & Hans Rystedt & Elin Johansson
summary_haiku: This study uses conversation analysis to examine 40 video-supported debriefings following simulation-based healthcare training. The research reveals that video enables students to discuss their interprofessional teamwork from a third-person perspective, while facilitators' instructional questions guide students to reconceptualize their performance by contrasting audiovisual appearances with their subjective experiences, facilitating collaborative sense-making about professional conduct.

title: Adaptable scripting to foster regulation processes and skills in
authors: Ingo Kollar & Karsten Stegmann & Xinghua Wang
summary_haiku: This study examined how adaptable collaboration scripts—which allow learners to modify script components based on self-perceived needs—affect regulation processes and skill acquisition in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a three-phase experimental design with 87 university students, results showed adaptable scripts significantly increased metacognitive reflection and monitoring activities compared to fixed scripts, and substantially improved learners' self-regulation skills in subsequent unscripted tasks. Mediation analyses revealed reflection processes during scripted collaboration explained the positive effects on later regulation skill transfer.

title: Life history of a topic in an online discussion: a complex systems theory perspective on how one message attracts class members to create meaning collaboratively
authors: Jane S. Vogler & Diane L. Schallert & Michelle E. Jordan & Kwangok Song & Anke J. Z. Sanders & Yueh-hui Yan Te Chiang & Ji-Eun Lee & Jeongbin Hannah Park & Li-Tang Yu
summary_haiku: This qualitative study applied complex adaptive systems theory to analyze how meaning emerges in synchronous online classroom discussions. Researchers tracked one pivotal message (#43) and its resulting topic through multiple data sources including transcripts, screen recordings, and video observations of eight graduate students. Findings revealed that interdependent processes and content co-create understanding, private individual meaning-making mingles with public shared experiences, and topics follow developmental trajectories from inception through decline, demonstrating how collaborative learning emerges through system-level interactions.

title: Joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: The A3C framework
authors: Ulrike Cress & Heisawn Jeong & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle
summary_haiku: This conceptual article proposes the A3C framework distinguishing four types of joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: Attendance, Coordination, Cooperation, and Collaboration. These interaction types vary by how members share goals, processes, and outcomes, progressing from individualistic orientations to fully shared endeavors. The framework integrates cognitive and socio-cultural perspectives to explain diverse participation patterns in mass-scale communities like Wikipedia and Scratch.

title: All in good time: knowledge introduction, restructuring, and development of shared opinions as different stages in collaborative writing
authors: Johannes Moskaliuk & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: This study examined how secondary school student dyads with differing theoretical perspectives on media effects collaborated to write shared texts. Using quantitative and qualitative content analysis of eight text versions, researchers identified three distinct sequential stages: early knowledge introduction, middle restructuring activities, and late shared opinion development. Results demonstrated that collaborative writing progresses through predictable phases, with different activities dominating each stage as participants integrate divergent perspectives into unified conclusions.

title: Facilitating socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning with a regulation macro script – an exploratory study
authors: Jaana Isohatala & Sanna Jarvela & Piia Naykki & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how a regulation macro script supports socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning among teacher education students. Using video analysis of 20 group sessions, researchers found that groups engaged more actively with orientation phases than intermediate or reflection phases. Active script discussions stimulated significantly more socio-emotional support provision than less active discussions. Importantly, socio-emotional support initiated during scripted phases transferred to subsequent unscripted task work, suggesting scripts can facilitate sustained collaborative regulation.

title: How to combine collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples to foster mathematical argumentation – when working memory matters
authors: Matthias Schwaighofer & Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Stefan Ufer & Anselm Strohmaier & Ilka Terwedow & Sarah Ottinger & Kristina Reiss
summary_haiku: This study examined how sequencing and fading collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples affect university students' mathematical argumentation skills. Using a 2×2 factorial design with 108 freshmen, researchers found that fading the initially presented scaffold improved dialogic skills regardless of sequence. For dialectic skills, working memory capacity moderated fading effects: low-capacity learners benefited most from fading the collaboration script when presented first, while high-capacity learners benefited from simultaneous scaffold availability.

title: Cracking her codes: understanding shared technology resources as positioning artifacts for power and status in CSCL environments
authors: Amber Simpson & Nicole Bannister & Gretchen Matthews
summary_haiku: Researchers used positioning theory and interaction analysis to examine how two pairs of female students negotiated power and status around shared technology during cryptography tasks. Analysis revealed that technology control functioned as a positioning artifact reflecting and reinforcing power dynamics: one pair exhibited stark dominance limiting participation, while the other showed subtle status imbalances without apparent learning impact. The study concludes that interactions around technology serve as critical indicators of negotiated power and status in collaborative learning environments.

title: Investigating the effects of peer to peer prompts on collaborative argumentation, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
authors: Owen M. Harney & Michael J. Hogan & Sarah Quinn
summary_haiku: Peer-driven prompts in computer-supported collaborative learning using Interactive Management significantly enhanced student outcomes compared to facilitator-driven prompts. With 101 undergraduate students across eight groups, peer-driven conditions produced higher perceived consensus, perceived efficacy, team orientation, and more sophisticated argumentation patterns, while reducing discomfort in group learning. Results demonstrate that structured peer prompting, supported through facilitator modeling and gradual responsibility transfer, effectively supports collaborative learning and critical thinking development.

title: The value of learning talk: applying a novel dialogue scoring method to inform interaction design in an open-ended, embodied museum exhibit
authors: Jessica Roberts
summary_haiku: # Summary Researchers developed SQuILD, a novel dialogue-scoring method for quantifying learning talk in open-ended museum exhibits. Testing this method on 119 visitor groups interacting with an interactive census data map, they compared full-body versus handheld tablet controls and single versus multi-user input configurations. Contrary to theoretical predictions, handheld tablet controls produced significantly higher-quality learning dialogue than full-body interaction, suggesting that intuitive, familiar interfaces may better support collaborative meaning-making than physically immersive designs.

title: Developing & using interaction geography in a museum
authors: Ben Rydal Shapiro & Rogers P. Hall & David A. Owens
summary_haiku: Researchers developed "interaction geography," an integrative approach combining conversation analysis, movement tracking, and spatial design to study visitor engagement in museum settings. Using Mondrian Transcription and the Interaction Geography Slicer visualization tool, they analyzed 22 visitor groups' complete museum visits. A CSCL environment enabled museum professionals to reframe their understanding of visitor behavior—particularly children's movement—from disruptive to purposeful learning, supporting evidence-based design decisions for equitable learning opportunities.

title: I think you just got mixed up: confident peer tutors hedge to support partners’ face needs
authors: Justine Cassell & Amy Ogan & Michael Madaio
summary_haiku: Peer tutors with lower social closeness to tutees provide more positive feedback and use indirect language when delivering instructions and comprehension-monitoring, but only when they possess high tutoring self-efficacy. Conversely, tutees benefit from hedged instructions and comprehension-monitoring specifically in low-rapport dyads, suggesting that interpersonal closeness reduces the need for indirectness while self-efficacy enables strategic face-threat mitigation.

title: Visions of CSCL: eight provocations for the future of the field
authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: CSCL faces critical identity and relevance questions through eight provocations: the field needs unified conceptual frameworks for diverse tools, should prioritize learner agency over scripting, rigorously define collaboration and community, address methodological divides, pursue computational approaches, prioritize learning analytics and adaptive support, expand to social media and large-scale environments, and reconsider its commitment to educational change through research-practice partnerships.

title: Exploring college English language learners’ self and social regulation of learning during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities
authors: You Su & Yanyan Li & Hening Hu & Carolyn P. Rose
summary_haiku: This study examined self and social regulation of learning among 60 Chinese college English language learners during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities. Using content analysis and sequential analysis of chat logs, researchers found that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring, evaluation, and emotional regulation than low-performing groups. Sequential analysis revealed high-performing groups exhibited bidirectional patterns between co-regulation and socially shared regulation, while low-performing groups repeated self-regulation patterns.

title: Learning to monitor and regulate collective thinking processes
authors: Yann Shiou Ong & Marcela Borge & Carolyn Penstein Rose
summary_haiku: Students using a computer-supported framework for monitoring collaborative discussions significantly improved discourse quality over ten weeks. The study examined 37 students across 13 teams engaging in five discussion sessions, comparing two reflective scripting conditions. Results showed teams enhanced collaborative processes through individual assessment of communication patterns followed by collective sense-making, with evidence-based reflection prompts yielding higher-quality discourse than future-thinking prompts.

title: Using technological functions on a multi-touch table and their affordances to counteract biases and foster collaborative problem solving
authors: Inga M. Bause & Irina R. Brich & Ann-Katrin Wesslein & Friedrich W. Hesse
summary_haiku: Multi-touch table support functions with affordances for moving, structuring, and merging information significantly enhanced collaborative problem-solving in hidden-profile tasks. University student triads using the collaboration support kit showed greater discussion intensity, more balanced information exchange, stronger mutual understanding indicators, and five times higher correct decision rates compared to standard conditions, demonstrating that intuitive technological affordances can overcome biases from prior preferences.

title: Connecting levels of activity with classroom network technology
authors: Tobin White
summary_haiku: Classroom network technology enables fluid transitions between individual, small-group, and whole-class mathematics instruction. Through design-based research analyzing two learning environments, this study identifies mechanisms—appropriation, mediation, emergence, and orchestration—that support multilevel activity. Findings reveal that rather than sequential shifts between levels, classroom activity often exhibits simultaneous, overlapping interactions across planes, with shared mathematical objects mediating connections between groups and facilitating dynamic classroom participation.

title: One framework to rule them all? Carrying forward the conversation started by Wise and Schwarz
authors: Nikol Rummel
summary_haiku: Rather than seeking one unified CSCL framework top-down, this article proposes using a 12-dimension taxonomy of support characteristics as a foundation for collaborative empirical research. Through experimental studies varying dimensions like timing and foundation of instruction, the author demonstrates how systematic investigation across taxonomy dimensions can generate evidence-based design principles for computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: Community technology mapping: inscribing places when everything is on the move
authors: Katie Headrick Taylor & Reed Stevens & Deborah Silvis
summary_haiku: Community Technology Mapping (CTM) combines interactive digital mapping with structured interviews to support children's reflection on spatiotemporal organization of technology use across daily routines. Through ethnographic analysis of twelve children's mapping activities in Google Earth, researchers identified three inscription processes: making places visible through wayfinding, making places coherent through narrative reconciliation, and making places mobile through dynamic interaction. CTM functions as both pedagogical tool for developing locative literacies and methodological innovation for examining children's place-based learning beyond home observations.

title: Orchestrating the emergence of conceptual learning: a case study in a geometry class
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Naomi Prusak & Osama Swidan & Adva Livny & Kobi Gal & Avi Segal
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study investigates whether teachers can orchestrate conceptual learning across multiple student groups working simultaneously on geometry tasks. Using SAGLET, a system that monitors parallel group work and alerts teachers to critical moments via machine learning, the researchers observed one experienced teacher guiding eight groups through challenging quadrilateral hierarchy problems. Analysis revealed five intervention types—collaboration encouragement, task supervision, justification requests, argumentation scaffolding, and social validation—with scaffolding being most frequent. Results demonstrate successful orchestration: seven of eight groups solved difficult tasks requiring abstract geometric reasoning, suggesting that real-time alerts and visibility tools enable adaptive guidance across multiple groups in classroom settings.

title: Learning through collaborative design of location-based games
authors: Jo Dugstad Wake & Frode Guribye & Barbara Wasson
summary_haiku: Students collaboratively designed location-based games to learn history using the SILO authoring tool. Through design-based research and video analysis, the study found that students engaged creatively with historical materials while making design decisions about game difficulty, narrative structure, and location placement. Students explicitly considered peer players' experiences, demonstrating accountability and responsibility in their design process.

title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
authors: Paul A. Kirschner & John Sweller & Femke Kirschner & Jimmy Zambrano R
summary_haiku: Cognitive load theory, traditionally focused on individual learning, is extended to collaborative learning by incorporating the concept of collective working memory and transactive activities. The authors argue that collaboration reduces cognitive load when tasks exceed individual working memory capacity, but transactive costs of communication and coordination can negate benefits. Design principles for effective collaborative learning must consider task complexity, team composition, prior experience, and domain expertise.

title: Challenges in online collaboration: effects of scripting shared task perceptions
authors: Allyson F. Hadwin & Aishah Bakhtiar & Mariel Miller
summary_haiku: This study examined how different types of planning visualizations affect collaborative learning challenges and regulatory strategies. Undergraduate students (N=180) completed collaborative tasks under three conditions: quantified visualization, nominal visualization, or no visualization of group members' planning perceptions. Results showed groups without visualization support reported greater planning challenge severity and experienced cascading difficulties across multiple challenge types. Groups receiving visualization support reported more effective strategy use. Findings support integrating planning awareness tools into computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups
authors: Kshitij Sharma & Bertrand Schneider & Sebastien Cuendet & Guillaume Zufferey & Pierre Dillenbourg & Roy Pea
summary_haiku: Mobile eye-trackers reveal that joint visual attention correlates with collaborative learning quality in co-located dyads, but high coordination alone doesn't guarantee learning. Qualitative analysis of two high-coordination groups showed that imbalanced participation—where one student dominates initiating joint attention—predicts lower learning gains, suggesting that productive collaboration requires balanced visual leadership between partners.

title: Why and how do middle school students exchange ideas during science inquiry?
authors: Camillia Matuk
summary_haiku: This study investigates how the Idea Manager tool supports middle school students' peer idea exchange during science inquiry on cancer and cell division. Using the Knowledge Integration framework with 297 grade 7 students, researchers found that students generated more ideas independently than copying peers' ideas, and that collecting redundant self-generated ideas correlated with higher-quality scientific explanations, contrary to expectations favoring diverse ideas. Teachers reported enhanced formative assessment capabilities through monitoring student progress.

title: Comparing effects of two collaboration scripts on learning activities for wiki-based environments
authors: Sven Heimbuch & Lisa Ollesch & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared two wiki collaboration scripts for educational knowledge construction. The Discuss-Deliberate-Revise (DDR) script, emphasizing upfront discussion before edits, was tested against Wikipedia's Be Bold-Revert-Discuss (BRD) script promoting frequent individual edits. Across a pre-study with dyads and main study with larger groups, DDR encouraged more discussion and produced higher-quality, error-free articles, though direct learning gains were minimal. Individual differences in cognitive closure, metacognitive strategies, and motivation moderated script effectiveness.

title: The opportunities of networks of research-practice partnerships and why CSCL should not give up on large-scale educational change
authors: Ornit Sagy & Yael Kali & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This article argues that CSCL should pursue large-scale educational change through networks of design-centric research-practice partnerships (DC-RPPs). The authors counter arguments that the field has abandoned this goal by demonstrating how collaborative networks integrating researchers, practitioners, and policymakers can generate scalable, sustainable innovations. They illustrate this approach through Taking Citizen Science to School, a five-year Israeli research center connecting citizen science with classroom learning.

title: Students’ engagement with real-time graphs in CSCL settings: scrutinizing the role of teacher support
authors: Line Ingulfsen & Anniken Furberg & Torunn Aanesland Stromme
summary_haiku: This study examined student-teacher interactions during collaborative real-time lab work on ocean acidification. Using interaction analysis of 49 student-teacher exchanges, researchers identified challenges students faced interpreting graphs and connecting experimental actions to scientific phenomena. The teacher provided crucial support through eliciting strategies—using gestures, prompts, and cued questions—and elaboration strategies, demonstrating how teacher guidance intersects with digital resources and instructional design to scaffold conceptual understanding in CSCL settings.

title: When coding-and-counting is not enough: using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze verbal data in CSCL research
authors: Brendan Eagan & Ingo Kollar & David Williamson Shaffer
summary_haiku: Traditional coding-and-counting analyses of collaborative learning discourse ignore temporal relationships between learning actions, potentially missing important patterns. This study compared traditional frequency-based analysis with Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), which models temporal co-occurrences of coded actions. Analyzing pre-service teachers' problem-solving discourse, ENA revealed that evidence evaluation was central to dyadic reasoning but not individual reasoning—a pattern invisible to traditional methods. Results confirm that temporal structure, not merely code frequency, drives these findings.

title: Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools
authors: Asa Makitalo & Thomas Hillman & Anne Solli
summary_haiku: Digital mapping tools developed for Science and Technology Studies enable upper secondary students to collaboratively explore controversial socioscientific issues online. Through video analysis of students using network visualization software (Gephi), researchers found that tool-mediated activity slowed categorization processes, prompting productive negotiation of how to interpret controversies. Misalignments between algorithmic tool logic and students' content-focused reasoning generated valuable collaborative discussion about distinguishing controversies from their visualizations.

title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
authors: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: Researchers analyzed Wikipedia using big data techniques—text classification, social network analysis, and clustering—to examine how "productive friction" (resolving socio-cognitive conflicts) drives learning and knowledge construction at both individual and collective levels. Findings demonstrated that knowledge development occurs when diverse contributors engage across different perspectives, while homogeneous groups risk polarization and stagnation.

title: Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: # Summary This experimental study with 260 university students examined how different types of group awareness information guide collaborative learning. Dyads discussed blood-sugar regulation while receiving either cognitive information about peers' assumptions, metacognitive information about peers' confidence levels, both, or neither. Results showed that visualized information strongly influenced task selection strategies—learners focused on conflicting assumptions or uncertain topics based on available information. However, providing awareness information did not significantly improve learning outcomes, suggesting that guiding study behavior alone may be insufficient without additional support for collaborative knowledge construction processes.

title: Instrumental genesis in the design studio
authors: Lucila Carvalho & Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Peter Goodyear
summary_haiku: Instrumental Genesis theory explains how artifacts and their uses co-evolve within specific environments. This study applies IG to the neglected "upstream" phase of CSCL design, examining how educational designers use design studio artifacts to create collaborative learning tasks. Through two empirical studies involving design teams using the CoCoDes tool and design patterns, the researchers traced how artifacts move downstream to learners and how designer practices move upstream to inform tool improvements, demonstrating CSCL design as a distributed, dynamic system of instrument-mediated activity.

title: Imagining with improvised representations in CSCL environments
authors: Magdalena Kersting & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: This study examines how upper secondary physics students collaboratively improvise and introduce representations outside designed learning environments to solve problems. Through video analysis of small groups using an interactive map task comparing two- and three-dimensional spatial representations, researchers identified emergent improvised representations including gestures, physical objects, and digital tools like GoogleEarth. Findings reveal that imagination—conceptualized as a social, embodied, and materially distributed process—enables students to recognize representational needs and discover new possibilities, with multimodal shifts facilitating sophisticated meaning-making across digital, physical, gestural, and dimensional boundaries.

title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
authors: Judith ter Vrugte & Anjo Anjewierden & Lars Bollen & Elise H. Eshuis & Jakob Sikken & Ton de Jong
summary_haiku: Combining conventional instruction with an online reflection tool incorporating self-assessment, peer feedback, and goal-setting significantly improved vocational students' collaborative behavior and knowledge acquisition in computer-supported learning environments. Analysis of chat logs and knowledge tests from 198 first-year technical students revealed that instruction alone proved ineffective, but instruction paired with the reflection tool fostered higher-quality collaboration and superior learning outcomes compared to control conditions.

title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic
authors: Yotam Hod & Ornit Sagy
summary_haiku: This study synthesizes 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis to clarify authentic learning design. The authors identify three cultures—current, authentic, and intended—operating in authentic learning environments and distinguish between simulation approaches (classroom-based enculturation) and hybrid approaches (direct practitioner interaction). A coding scheme analyzing participants, settings, time, computer support, and collaboration reveals that timeframe most clearly differentiates approaches, offering CSCL designers a refined conceptual framework and visualization tool for understanding authentic learning environment variations.

title: Towards a micro-ecological approach to CSCL
authors: Marcela Borge
summary_haiku: # Summary Current CSCL theories prioritize single-level analysis, limiting understanding of complex orchestration processes. This paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels simultaneously. Through a design club case study, the authors identify "transecological disruptions"—critical moments where actions at one level propagate across levels—demonstrating how this approach reveals orchestration complexity and learning opportunities that traditional single-level analyses miss.

title: Learners’ agency and CSCL technologies: towards an emancipatory perspective
authors: future of CSCL
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that CSCL should adopt an emancipatory perspective prioritizing learners' agency over technology-imposed constraints. Tchounikine proposes that learners should be empowered to select, adapt, and interoperate software applications while receiving informed feedback. The analysis identifies key challenges: enabling technology choice, supporting customization, and providing transparent information—requiring fundamental reconceptualization of CSCL technologies as services rather than fixed applications.

title: Deliberative emotional talk
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: This study demonstrates that high-quality deliberative discussions about controversial issues can integrate strong emotions with argumentative rigor. Using design-based research, the authors developed the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP), a CSCL tool enabling teachers to design, moderate, and reflect on emotionally-engaged discussions. Through a 30-hour professional development course with 25 teachers, analysis revealed teachers recognize emotions as essential to democratic education and develop sophisticated moderation practices balancing authentic expression with critical thinking standards, establishing proof-of-concept for "deliberative emotional talk."

title: Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going?
authors: Frank P. C. M. de Jong & Jan van Aalst & Natascha de Hoog & Hennie van Heijst & Paul A. Kirschner
summary_haiku: This study analyzes socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge-building discourse among Master's students using a framework with four social and four cognitive components. Analyzing 638 Knowledge Forum contributions, researchers found moderate openness levels with higher social than cognitive openness. Cognitive openness indicators—particularly elaboration, justification, and inviting response—positively predicted follow-up contributions, while social openness showed no significant relationship. Expressing uncertainty emerged as key to sustaining knowledge-building conversations.

title: Guiding collaborative revision of science explanations
authors: Libby Gerard & Ady Kidron
summary_haiku: Combining automated explanation scoring with teacher guidance in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment, this study examined how one sixth-grade teacher customized adaptive feedback to guide 98 student pairs in revising science explanations about plate tectonics. Analysis of classroom interactions revealed five distinct teacher guidance strategies that leveraged automated scores to personalize support. Results showed nearly all pairs engaged in meaningful revision, with significant improvements in explanation quality and individual posttest gains, demonstrating how teacher-computer partnerships can effectively promote collaborative knowledge integration.

title: Supporting classroom orchestration with real-time feedback: A role for teacher dashboards and real-time agents
authors: Mike Tissenbaum & Jim Slotta
summary_haiku: This design-based research study investigates how real-time software agents and teacher dashboards support orchestration of complex collaborative physics inquiry in high school classrooms. Using the Knowledge Community and Inquiry model, researchers developed SAIL Smart Space technology with four agent types to dynamically manage student grouping, material allocation, and teacher notifications. Results demonstrate that the tablet-based orchestration system successfully reduced teacher workload while enabling timely interventions that significantly improved student problem-solving outcomes.

title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
authors: Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven & Jennifer K. Olsen
summary_haiku: This study compared combined collaborative-individual learning to either approach alone using an intelligent tutoring system for fractions with 382 elementary students. Results showed the combined condition produced higher learning gains than individual or collaborative-only conditions, particularly for fourth graders. Process data revealed combined-condition students made fewer errors and requested fewer hints, while reporting greater situational interest in the activity.

title: A handheld classroom dashboard: Teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study examined four teachers' perspectives on using a real-time analytics dashboard during 72 classroom sessions over ten weeks in a multi-tabletop collaborative learning environment. The handheld dashboard displayed group participation, task progress, script enactment, and automatically detected misconceptions. Through semi-structured interviews, teachers reported that visualizations enhanced awareness and decision-making, though they identified tensions regarding data incompleteness, immediate versus delayed feedback, orchestration load, and device portability, highlighting critical design considerations for effective CSCL classroom analytics tools.

title: Real-time orchestrational technologies in
authors: Camillia Matuk & Michael Tissenbaum
summary_haiku: Real-time dashboards in computer-supported collaborative learning environments enable teachers to monitor student progress and provide timely, targeted guidance during complex collaborative activities. This special issue examines five empirical studies investigating how real-time data visualization supports classroom orchestration, finding that effective designs partner with teachers rather than replace their functions, balance automated support with teacher autonomy, and require participatory design involving educators throughout development.

title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
authors: Anouschka van Leeuwen & Nikol Rummel & Tamara van Gog
summary_haiku: Teachers struggle to interpret collaborative learning situations from dashboards. This experimental study (n=53) compared three dashboard types—mirroring, alerting, and advising—examining how different support levels affect teachers' detection and interpretation of student collaboration problems in fraction tasks. Results showed dashboard type did not influence detection speed or accuracy, but advising dashboards significantly improved interpretation depth, with teachers adopting more analytical stances toward situations.

title: Correction to: A handheld classroom dashboard: teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This correction notice addresses duplicate images in the original article examining teachers' perspectives on a handheld classroom dashboard for real-time collaborative learning analytics. The correction republishes the correct versions of Figures 4 and 6, which display visualizations of group task progress, individual participation, and real-time feedback on learning design enactment.

title: Cohesion in online environments
authors: Maria Altebarmakian & Richard Alterman
summary_haiku: Online group cohesion emerges from students' engagement choices in asynchronous collaboration. This case study analyzed 29 students completing design assignments through a custom platform, measuring cohesion via behavioral engagement, interactivity, and cognitive engagement. Results show students prioritized thoughtful commenting over interactive dialogue, achieving moderate cohesion sufficient for reflective meaning-making but limited direct negotiation of ideas.

title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
authors: Hanna Jarvenoja
summary_haiku: This review examines methodological progress in researching socially shared regulation (SSRL) of learning in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning contexts. The authors identify three key challenges: capturing regulation's cyclical, temporal nature; understanding how self-regulation, co-regulation, and SSRL jointly contribute to learning; and studying SSRL in authentic contexts. They advocate for multimodal data collection methods, technological tools for prompting regulation, and analyzing learning challenges as triggers for regulatory processes.

title: Are we together or not? The temporal interplay of monitoring, physiological arousal and physiological synchrony during a collaborative exam
authors: Jonna Malmberg & Eetu Haataja & Tapio Seppanen & Sanna Jarvela
summary_haiku: This study examined metacognitive monitoring during collaborative exams using video analysis and physiological sensors measuring electrodermal activity. Results showed all group members contributed to monitoring, with monitoring frequency significantly correlating with physiological arousal peaks. Physiological synchrony occurred in groups experiencing task difficulties, suggesting it may indicate meaningful collaborative learning events requiring intervention.

title: Distributed spatial Sensemaking on the augmented reality sandbox
authors: Yotam Hod & Daniel Twersky
summary_haiku: This study uses Interaction Analysis to examine how small collaborative groups engage in distributed spatial sensemaking while using an Augmented Reality Sandbox for topographical learning. Findings reveal that AR features (contour lines, water simulations) coordinated with a 2D monitor representation enable groups to rapidly develop intrinsic-dynamic spatial thinking, facilitate quick trouble-repair sequences, and support divergent-to-convergent turn-taking patterns essential for advancing spatial understanding.

title: Learning in embodied activity framework: a sociocultural framework for embodied cognition
authors: Joshua A. Danish & Noel Enyedy & Asmalina Saleh & Megan Humburg
summary_haiku: This paper proposes the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework (LEAF), which synthesizes individual and sociocultural theories to explain how bodies support collaborative learning. Using Cultural Historical Activity Theory, the authors analyze data from the Science through Technology Enhanced Play project, where first and second-grade students used mixed-reality simulations to learn about particle behavior and states of matter. LEAF extends embodied cognition research by explicitly examining how individual and collective embodied actions, mediated by tools, rules, community, and division of labor, jointly shape learning in collaborative contexts.

title: Unpacking the relationship between existing and new measures of physiological synchrony and collaborative learning: a mixed methods study
authors: Bertrand Schneider
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined how electrodermal activity (EDA) measures physiological synchrony in collaborative learning. Forty-two dyads programmed robots while wearing EDA sensors. Pearson's correlation and directional agreement showed modest associations with learning gains and collaboration quality. Qualitative analysis of high and low-performing groups revealed that synchrony peaks during external events, oscillates during collaboration, and drops during independent work. A novel measure—cycles between low and high synchrony—strongly correlated with collaboration quality and learning outcomes, suggesting it captures distinct collaborative dynamics.

title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Anika Radkowitsch & Freydis Vogel & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This meta-analysis of 53 studies examined computer-supported collaboration scripts' effects on learner outcomes. Results showed scripts produced non-significant positive effects on motivation, small positive effects on domain learning, and medium positive effects on collaboration skills. Contrary to widespread criticism, scripts did not undermine motivation. However, combining multiple collaborative activity prompts generally reduced effectiveness compared to single-activity scripts, suggesting simpler designs may be more beneficial for learning.

title: Does collaborative learning design align with enactment? An innovative method of evaluating the alignment in the CSCL context
authors: Lanqin Zheng & Panpan Cui
summary_haiku: This study proposes design-centered research (DCR), a novel quantitative methodology for evaluating alignment between collaborative learning designs and their actual enactment. Using three indicators—activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, and interactive approach—plus interaction path graphs, researchers analyzed 40 groups across two iterations. Results show significant alignment improvements in round two after design optimization, with corresponding gains in group performance, demonstrating that data-driven design refinement enhances collaborative learning effectiveness.

title: Talking about group (but not individual) process aids group performance
authors: Noel Capon & Hueiyi Lai & Deanna Kuhn
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how group discourse relates to collaborative problem-solving performance. Graduate business students worked in small groups through a computer-supported marketing simulation over eight sessions. Discourse analysis revealed that groups discussing their collective process (Meta-group talk) achieved superior outcomes, while talk focused on individual perspectives (Meta-self talk) correlated negatively with performance. Meta-group discourse included understanding others, defining group position, planning, and evaluating—functions that facilitate coordinated action essential for effective collaboration.

title: Regulating self-organized collaborative learning: the importance of homogeneous problem perception, immediacy and intensity of strategy use
authors: Martin Greisel & Markus Dresel & Ingo Kollar & Nadine Melzner
summary_haiku: Self-organized study groups achieve greater satisfaction when members develop shared problem perceptions, apply strategies that directly address identified problems, and use regulation strategies frequently. This longitudinal study of 122 university students across 52 groups examined how problem perception homogeneity, strategy immediacy, and strategy intensity predict satisfaction with collaborative learning experiences during exam preparation, confirming all three hypotheses through hierarchical linear modeling.

title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Olga Viberg & Henriikka Vartiainen
summary_haiku: This study validates social network analysis centrality measures for analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning. Using data from 12 university courses with 598 students, researchers examined how different network configurations (multigraph, simplified, weighted) affect the reproducibility of centrality measures as indicators of student performance. Results show multigraph configuration produces the most consistent and robust measures, with degree centralities reliably indicating participation and eigenvector centrality consistently reflecting social dimensions across configurations.

title: Finding a place for equity in CSCL: ambitious learning practices as a lever for sustained educational change
authors: Suraj Uttamchandani & Ayesha Bhimdiwala & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) should prioritize educational equity by implementing ambitious learning practices—pedagogies emphasizing collaboration, dialogue, and disciplinary engagement. The authors contend that centering equity through student agency, shared meaning-making, and disruption of social inequality positions CSCL to meaningfully contribute to sustained educational change. They examine adaptive collaborative learning support as a case study, highlighting tensions between technological structure and learner agency while proposing that CSCL innovations can support equitable educational transformation when equity considerations guide development throughout.

title: Encouraging collaboration and building Community in Online Asynchronous Professional Development: designing for social capital
authors: Susan A. Yoon & Katherine Miller & Thomas Richman & Daniel Wendel & Ilana Schoenfeld & Emma Anderson & Jooeun Shim
summary_haiku: This study examined how online asynchronous professional development designed around social capital mechanisms supports science teachers' learning. Eight high school biology teachers participated in a six-week course combining discussion prompts, expert videos, and peer facilitation. Satisfaction surveys showed high ratings across all dimensions. Transactivity analysis revealed that collaborative prompts significantly increased peer interaction compared to content or implementation prompts. Interview data indicated positive perceptions of expertise access and interaction depth, though trust-building remained challenging in the asynchronous format.

title: Data wrangling practices and collaborative interactions with aggregated data
authors: Shiyan Jiang & Jennifer Kahn
summary_haiku: Youth engaged in data wrangling—selecting and managing large datasets to create models and stories—using interactive visualization tools to explore family migration. Analysis of talk-in-interaction identified ten sociotechnical practices and four learning activity categories: addressing missing data, understanding aggregation, exploring historical events, and varying visual encoding. Collaborative interactions with instructors and peers supported critical inquiry and meaning-making about data's social significance.

title: Dialogic intervisualizing in multimodal inquiry
authors: Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Lap Ki Chan & Judith L. Green & Susan M. Bridges & Asmalina Saleh
summary_haiku: Medical students collaboratively constructed understanding of cardiovascular physiology through facilitated problem-based learning using multimodal digital texts. Using Interactional Ethnography to analyze one PBL cycle, researchers traced how students iteratively accessed, curated, and generated visual representations—from simple diagrams to complex cardiac cycle charts—within dialogic exchanges with their facilitator. The study proposes "dialogic intervisualizing" as a theoretical construct characterizing dynamic interplay between information problem-solving, textual negotiation, and purposeful dialogue for deep knowledge co-construction in computer-supported inquiry.

title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
authors: Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen & Sini Riikonen
summary_haiku: This study examined how seventh-grade student teams engaged in collaborative making projects using digital and traditional fabrication technologies. Researchers developed the Making-Process-Rug video analysis method to trace social-discursive and materially mediated aspects of five teams' co-invention processes. Four successful teams demonstrated iterative cycles integrating model making with focused discussion, while the unsuccessful team lacked substantive prototyping. Shared epistemic objects and well-organized collaboration processes proved essential for successful co-invention.

title: Give student ideas a larger stage: support cross-community interaction for knowledge building
authors: Guangji Yuan & Maria Bogouslavsky & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: Two grade 5/6 science classrooms engaged in knowledge building about human body systems using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks. Students created "super notes"—synthesized summaries of inquiry progress—as epistemic boundary objects shared in a cross-classroom meta-space. Qualitative analysis revealed students conceived super notes as refined, accessible "big ideas" reflecting their learning journey. Super notes facilitated cross-community interaction, enabling students to encounter diverse perspectives, deepen inquiry, and develop integrated system-level understandings, demonstrating how scaling CSCL practices across classrooms fosters high-level epistemic engagement.

title: A review of the International Handbook of
authors: Jeremy Roschelle
summary_haiku: This review examines the International Handbook of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 2020, analyzing its contributions to the thirty-year-old CSCL field. Using Kuhn's paradigm shift framework, the author identifies the handbook as both a consensus document summarizing established theories, designs, and methods, and a source of productive disequilibria—unresolved tensions in diversity/equity, scalability, learning analytics integration, and methodological coherence—that present opportunities for transformative scholarship and paradigm shifts.

title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
authors: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen
summary_haiku: This sociocultural study examined how students' collaborative knowledge practices are mediated multimodally in a school makerspace during STEAM challenges. Through discourse and multimodal interaction analysis of 350 minutes of video data from two student groups, researchers identified four intertwined knowledge practices: orienting to, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge. Findings reveal that discourse, materials, embodied actions, and spatial arrangements jointly mediated students' joint attention and knowledge creation, with peer guidance proving more influential than teacher support or pre-given instructions.

title: Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning
authors: Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley & Ton de Jong & Maria Jesus Rodriguez-Triana & Denis Gillet
summary_haiku: This large-scale study analyzed 40,235 inquiry learning designs created in Graasp, an online platform used by 35,000+ teachers, to examine how social practices relate to classroom implementation of pedagogical innovations. Using the Knowledge Appropriation Model framework, researchers found that knowledge maturation, expert scaffolding, and knowledge appropriation practices were significantly associated with increased adoption rates of learning designs in classrooms, with maturation showing the strongest effect.

title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
authors: Yugo Hayashi
summary_haiku: A 2×2 experimental study examined how real-time gaze feedback and pedagogical conversational agent suggestions independently and jointly affect collaborative learning. Eighty dyads completed a knowledge integration task while receiving various combinations of these interventions. Results showed gaze feedback more effectively facilitated coordination processes, while agent suggestions better improved learning gains. Combined interventions produced synergistic effects on performance, with successful coordination strongly predicting learning outcomes only when both supports were present.

title: The spiral model of collaborative knowledge improvement: an exploratory study of a networked collaborative classroom
authors: Wenli Chen & Jesmine S. H. Tan & Zhongling Pi
summary_haiku: This exploratory case study introduces the Spiral Model of Collaborative Knowledge Improvement (SMCKI), a five-phase pedagogical framework designed to scaffold multi-layered collaborative learning in networked classrooms. Pre-service teachers collaboratively designed technology-enhanced learning activities through individual ideation, intra-group synergy, inter-group critique, intra-group refinement, and individual achievement phases. Results demonstrate significant quality improvements in technology-enhanced learning designs across all SMCKI phases, with participants progressively advancing from simple to complex knowledge dimensions.

title: Capturing regulatory patterns in online collaborative learning: A network analytic approach
authors: Si Zhang & Juan Chen & Yun Wen & Hongxian Chen & Qianqian Gao & Qiyun Wang
summary_haiku: This study examined 45 student teachers' regulatory patterns during online collaborative learning using content analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA). Findings revealed that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring and emotional regulation behaviors than low-performing groups across different activity stages. The analysis identified distinct regulatory patterns: high-performing groups emphasized planning and evaluation, while low-performing groups relied on routine-level regulatory strategies throughout collaboration.

title: Affording embodied cognition through touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative tabletop science learning
authors: Nikita Soni
summary_haiku: This study examined how family groups use touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative learning with multi-touch tabletops displaying ocean temperature data. Using a user-centered design approach, researchers analyzed 11 family groups' utterances and gestures to identify embodied cognition instances. Four gesture types emerged: orienting the group, cooperative gestures, individual intentional gestures, and articulating conceptual understanding. Findings reveal specific gestural interactions that facilitate embodied-cognition-supported collaborative meaning-making in science learning.

title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
authors: Sebastian Strauss & Nikol Rummel
doi: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
summary_haiku: This field experiment examined whether combining a group awareness tool (GAT) with adaptive prompts supports equal participation in online collaborative learning. Sixty-one students in groups received either no support, a GAT alone, or GAT plus prompts. While students showed higher satisfaction with more equal participation, the collaboration support produced only tentative effects on participation equality. Groups initiating collaboration early and coordinating continuously achieved better participation distribution and satisfaction, suggesting interaction patterns matter more than the technological interventions tested.

title: Net.Create: Network Visualization to Support Collaborative Historical Knowledge Building
authors: Kalani Craig & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Cindy Hmelo-Silver & Maksymilian Szostalo & Ann McCranie
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines Net.Create, a collaborative network visualization tool designed to help undergraduate history students analyze complex texts. Using activity theory, researchers analyzed how the tool and accompanying activities help students reconcile contradictions between detail and context, active learning and large lectures, and memorization versus historical reasoning. Analysis of log data, video recordings, and student papers from 76 students reveals that quality of historical significance annotations—not quantity of entries—correlates with stronger final papers. Students successfully moved between local details and aggregate patterns, with high-performing groups engaging in deeper "why" analysis compared to low-performing groups focused on "who" and "what."

title: Social sensitivity: a manifesto for CSCL research
authors: Jaana Isohatala & Piia Naykki & Sanna Jarvela & Michael J. Baker & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: Current educational technologies inadequately support collaborative learning as both cognitive and socio-emotional processes, risking hindered idea exchange and negative interactions. This manifesto argues CSCL research is fragmented across theoretical silos, failing to communicate coherent evidence to practitioners and developers. The authors propose "social sensitivity"—an interdisciplinary framework emphasizing constructively critical, respectful, and cohesive collaboration—and call for concrete actions: crossing theoretical boundaries, conducting multimodal empirical research, and transferring evidence to educational practices and policies.

title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
authors: Julia Eberle & Karsten Stegmann & Alain Barrat & Frank Fischer & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: This study examined how researchers initiate scientific collaborations at face-to-face academic events using network analysis of behavioral data. Analyzing 5,736 relations among 287 researchers at two technology-enhanced learning conferences, the researchers employed RFID devices to measure contact duration and social network questionnaires to identify collaboration intentions. Results revealed that longer face-to-face contact, reciprocity, and transitivity significantly predicted new collaboration formation. PhD students were less frequently selected as partners, and Information Technology researchers selected fewer partners overall. Group awareness support reduced disciplinary differences in partner selection, suggesting targeted interventions can facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
authors: Lisa Ollesch & Sven Heimbuch & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This study examined how cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools affect wiki-based collaborative learning through a 2×2 factorial experiment with 158 participants. Results show both tool types influence thread selection and discussion engagement, with behavioral awareness particularly motivating contributions. Critically, only the combination of cognitive and behavioral awareness improved article quality, suggesting complementary effects outweigh individual benefits in supporting wiki-based learning outcomes.

title: Guidance in computer‑supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
authors: Tarja Pietarinen & Tuire Palonen & Marja Vauras
summary_haiku: Teachers in computer-supported collaborative science inquiry learning primarily focused on task management and content knowledge while extensively observing groups. Mixed-methods analysis of four classrooms revealed teachers preferentially guided groups perceived as motivated and collaborative, regardless of prior competence. Notably, socio-emotional support was minimal. Teachers' positive affect correlated with student affect, suggesting reciprocal emotional influences on learning outcomes.

title: Prompting collaborative and exploratory discourse: An epistemic network analysis study
authors: Zarifa Zakaria & Jennifer Tsan & Anna Iwanski & Jessica Vandenberg & Collin Lynch & Kristy Elizabeth Boyer & Eric Wiebe
summary_haiku: This study examined how simple prompting interventions affect elementary students' collaborative discourse during pair programming. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to analyze coded dialogue from 62 fourth graders, researchers compared intervention students receiving empirically-derived prompts supporting exploratory talk with control students. Results revealed intervention students significantly increased justification, alternative ideas, and simple questions, demonstrating qualitatively different collaboration patterns through network visualizations showing stronger connections between exploratory talk codes.

title: The impact of a gamified mobile question‑asking app on museum visitor group interactions: an ICAP framing
authors: Jesse Ha & Luis E. Perez Cortes & Man Su & Brian C. Nelson & Catherine Bowman & Judd D. Bowman
summary_haiku: This study examined how a gamified mobile question-asking app affects museum visitor group interactions using the ICAP framework. Researchers compared two app modes—Ask Mode (baseline) and Game Mode (gamified)—across 1,539 visitor groups at two museums. Results showed gamified versions significantly increased group discussion frequency and collaborative question-asking, particularly among family groups and when children controlled the device, supporting mobile apps' potential for fostering informal collaborative learning.

title: Agency to transform: how did a grade 5 community co‑configure dynamic knowledge building practices in a yearlong science inquiry?
authors: Dan Tao & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: This study investigates how a fifth-grade science classroom co-configured dynamic knowledge-building practices through "reflective structuration"—a process where students and teacher collaboratively constructed and adapted shared inquiry structures over a yearlong human body systems investigation. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, online discourse, and student artifacts, researchers documented how students co-formulated nine evolving "big questions" that guided inquiry directions. Analysis revealed students' agentic moves expanded, deepened, and reframed collective work, with social network analysis and pre-post testing demonstrating productive knowledge building outcomes and improved scientific understanding.

title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
authors: Ishari Amarasinghe & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & H. Ulrich Hoppe
summary_haiku: This study compared how mirroring and guiding support in teacher dashboards influence orchestration load during scripted collaborative learning. Six teachers conducted Pyramid-pattern activities under three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring support, and guiding support with alerts. Using epistemic network analysis, researchers found that guiding support enabled more targeted interactions and announcements compared to mirroring support. The findings deconstruct orchestration load into situation evaluation, goal formation, and action-taking facets.

title: The trade‑off between individuals and groups: role interactions under different technology affordance conditions
authors: Cixiao Wang & Shuling Li
summary_haiku: This study examined how technology affordances—specifically device-to-student ratios (1:1 versus 1:m) and external scripts—influence role-based interactions during collaborative scientific inquiry. Using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and social network analysis with 130 fifth-grade students across three inquiry experiments, researchers identified eleven emergent roles organized into five categories. Key findings revealed that limited technology resources and external scripts promoted collective awareness, while personal device ownership encouraged individual-focused behavior. Stable group action orientations facilitated better coordination and learning outcomes, though close interaction density did not guarantee collaborative effectiveness.

title: Educational dialogues and computer supported collaborative learning: critical analysis and research perspectives
authors: Michael J. Baker & Baruch B. Schwarz & Sten R. Ludvigsen
