summary_haiku: This critical analysis proposes that educational dialogue research in CSCL requires theoretically grounded integration of diverse data types across multiple timescales. The authors argue the object of study should be collective thinking development in dialogue, with the exchange as the basic analytical unit. They introduce digital platforms as an intermediary analytical level between micro-dialogic exchanges and macro-institutional contexts, emphasizing the need for coherent theoretical frameworks connecting automatic and human analyses to avoid fragmentation.

title: Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
summary_haiku: This large-scale study of 69 courses (3,277 students) examines whether diffusion-based network centrality measures capture information exchange and predict academic success in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using meta-analysis across all courses, the research demonstrates that diffusion centralities—measuring how ideas spread through networks—show stronger and more consistent correlations with student achievement than traditional network measures. Clustering analysis identified three student roles: influencers, mediators, and isolates, validated through manual coding of interactions.

title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno
summary_haiku: This study identifies three distinct multi-modal behavioral profiles of dyads engaged in collaborative open-ended learning with interactive tabletops and a robot mediator. Using combined learning analytics and interaction analysis on video, audio, and log data from 32 teams, researchers discovered two learning profiles—Expressive Explorers and Calm Tinkerers—and one non-learning profile, Silent Wanderers. Key findings reveal that speech overlap and reflection behaviors strongly distinguish learners from non-learners, while problem-solving strategy interacts with emotional expressivity to characterize different pathways to learning.

title: Self‑efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real‑time collaboration system developed for group programming
authors: Ting-Chia Hsu & Hal Abelson & Evan Patton & Shih-Chu Chen & Hsuan-Ning Chang
summary_haiku: This study examined how adult learners' self-efficacy and collaborative behaviors differ when using a real-time collaboration (RTC) system integrated with MIT App Inventor for block-based programming. Using sequential behavior analysis on 13 participants grouped by disciplinary background, researchers found that RTC enabled simultaneous task execution and enhanced communication through annotations. Computer Science majors in homogeneous groups demonstrated significantly higher programming self-efficacy during collaboration than non-majors and heterogeneous groups, though individual versus collaborative self-efficacy remained comparable overall.

title: Integrating a collaboration script and group awareness to support group regulation and emotions towards collaborative problem solving
authors: Matias Rojas & Miguel Nussbaum & Orlando Guerrero & Pablo Chiuminatto & Samuel Greiff & Rodrigo Del Rio & Danilo Alvares
summary_haiku: This study examined how a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools affects elementary students' collaborative problem-solving skills. Using a quasi-experimental design with 223 sixth-graders, researchers compared an experimental group playing a six-level collaborative game to a control group receiving regular instruction. Results showed the intervention significantly improved attitudes toward collaboration and increased shared regulation and co-regulation processes. Qualitative analysis revealed positive emotions like satisfaction emerged through co-regulation, suggesting collaboration scripts combined with group awareness effectively support regulation skills and emotional development during collaborative problem-solving.

title: Supporting children’s place-based observations and explanations using collaboration scripts while learning-on- the-move outdoors
authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land
summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined how collaboration scripts embedded in a mobile augmented reality app supported children's learning during outdoor activities. Across two iterations with 87 youth participants, researchers found significant gains in tree life cycle knowledge for both groups. Iteration B, which included additional scripts for socially-shared regulation of learning, showed improved collaborative sense-making where children better coordinated observational evidence with explanations, though knowledge gains were comparable between iterations.

title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self‑regulation in computer‑supported collaborative learning
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Freydis Vogel
summary_haiku: This special issue examines three interconnected concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: group awareness, collaboration scripts, and self-regulation. Through conceptual and empirical papers, the collection explores how these mechanisms—which support learners' social interactions, cognitive processes, and metacognitive monitoring—can be combined to enhance collaborative learning design. The papers demonstrate that integrating these approaches yields more effective CSCL environments than addressing them separately.

title: Group awareness and regulation in
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This article conceptualizes group awareness (GA) in computer-supported collaborative learning as a conscious, current, individual cognitive construct about social entities that learners perceive as valid. The authors identify six defining aspects of GA and propose it operates within three regulatory cycles: regulating GA itself through metacognitive monitoring, regulating social interaction based on GA, and regulating partner schema building. The framework connects GA to working memory processes and suggests implications for designing support tools and conducting empirical research on collaborative learning mechanisms.

title: Adaptable scaffolding of mathematical argumentation skills: The role of self‑regulation when scaffolded with CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples
authors: Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer & Kristina Reiss & Stefan Ufer
summary_haiku: Two experiments examined adaptable versus non-adaptable scaffolding for mathematical argumentation skills in collaborative learning. University students (N=167) learned with either adaptable or fixed CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples. Results showed maximal scaffolding supported domain-specific skills, while adaptable scaffolds benefited students with higher self-regulation abilities. Self-regulation skills proved crucial for effectively utilizing adaptable scaffolding, particularly for socio-discursive argumentation development.

title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading’
authors: Jolique Kielstra & Inge Molenaar & Roel van Steensel & Ludo Verhoeven
summary_haiku: A collaboration script designed to support socially shared regulation during task-oriented reading facilitated mainly low-level metacognitive discussions among 44 prevocational students working in groups. While the script elicited metacognitive regulation through role-based information distribution, deep-level co-construction remained rare. However, students individually improved their ability to recognize high-level task characteristics and reflect on appropriate reading strategies post-intervention.

title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
authors: Charles Crook
summary_haiku: This commentary examines three foundational concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness. Through analysis of five special issue papers, Crook proposes that regulation operates in layered structures requiring "meta-metacognition," and that group awareness involves both social cognition and intersubjectivity. He reconceptualizes scripted collaboration using a theatre metaphor, emphasizing performance, direction, and audience perspectives to better integrate these concepts within classroom ecosystems.

title: A classification of Challenges encountered in Complex Teamwork Settings
authors: Maedeh A. Kazemitabar & Susanne P. Lajoie & Tianshu Li
summary_haiku: This study examined teamwork challenges in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment using a hackathon as the research context. Through multimodal data collection including questionnaires, interviews, and video recordings of 48 participants, researchers employed qualitative theory-driven coding to identify 16 distinct challenges. These challenges were categorized into seven macro-level themes: cognitive, motivational, emotional, behavioral, cognitive/behavioral, general, and external. The analysis revealed which challenges specifically impede mutual trust and shared mental models—key team coordination mechanisms—providing educators with insights for supporting effective collaboration in CSCL settings.

title: Cross-community knowledge building with idea thread mapper
authors: Guangji Yuan & Jianwei Zhang & Mei-Hwa Chen
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study investigated how four Grade 5 classrooms collaboratively built knowledge about human body systems using the Idea Thread Mapper (ITM) platform. Students engaged in local classroom inquiry while generating "super notes"—reflective syntheses—shared in a cross-community meta-space. Through cross-classroom "Super Talk" discussions on how people grow, students integrated diverse ideas from multiple classrooms into sophisticated, multifaceted understandings. Results demonstrated that students produced high-quality reflections and that cross-community collaboration created expansive learning contexts enabling knowledge advancement across social levels.

title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
authors: Shupin Li & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
summary_haiku: This study examined 166 Finnish sixth graders' action transition patterns during computer-based collaborative problem-solving using social network analysis. Researchers created transition networks from log file data and calculated network measures including density, centralization, and reciprocity. Results showed pairs with at least one member possessing high social and cognitive skills conducted significantly more actions with higher transition frequencies, suggesting more productive collaborative problem-solving than other pair compositions.

title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Daner Sun & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: This study examined how collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment enhances pre-service teachers' competencies in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building. Using a quasi-experimental design with 40 experimental and 28 comparison pre-service teachers over 18 weeks, the experimental group engaged in knowledge building enriched by KBDeX visualizations and rubrics, while the comparison group used portfolio assessment. Analysis of Knowledge Forum discourse revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher-level epistemic engagement, collaborative interactions, and metacognitive reflection. Epistemic network analysis showed stronger connections between higher-level actions in the experimental group, and cumulative degree centrality indicated greater community knowledge advancement. Results suggest collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment effectively scaffolds pre-service teachers' development of collaborative inquiry competencies.

title: iTalk–iSee: A participatory visual learning analytical tool for productive peer talk
authors: Liru Hu & Jiajun Wu & Gaowei Chen
summary_haiku: iTalk–iSee is a participatory visual learning analytics tool designed to support primary school students' productive peer talk in dialogic collaborative problem-solving. Grounded in Bakhtinian dialogism theory, the tool maps 18 productive talk moves onto three DCPS goals (equality/respect, open-mindedness, convergence) and employs visualization design principles with a three-step macro-script (code→visualize→reflect) to strengthen learner agency. Field study evaluation with 59 fourth-graders demonstrated usability improvements through iterative refinement and positive user experience ratings.

title: Shared meaning-making in online intergroup discussions around sensitive topics
authors: Tugce Aldemir & Marcela Borge & Jose Soto
summary_haiku: This study identifies four communication patterns associated with multicultural collaborative competence (MCC) in online intergroup discussions about sensitive identity topics: grounding with narratives, exploring differences and commonalities, critical reflection, and emotional support. Through qualitative analysis of four undergraduate teams' discussions, the researchers found that existing general collaborative competence frameworks inadequately capture these socio-political dynamics, though some overlap exists between MCC sophistication and traditional collaboration quality measures.

title: Fostering growth orientations in students’ identities as knowledge builders
authors: Shiri Kashi & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This study examined how students develop growth orientations in humanistic knowledge building communities (HKBCs). Using grounded analysis of 322 utterances from graduate students' reflective diaries and discussions, researchers identified five dimensions of fixedness-growth orientations: feelings, mindset, personal responsibility, self-constructs, and attitudes toward change. Statistical analysis revealed significant increases in growth orientation across the semester. Case studies illustrated how students transformed from fixed to growth orientations through community support and reflection, with implications for self-regulated learning and emergent roles in collaborative environments.

title: Implementing learning analytics in wiki-supported collaborative learning in secondary education: A framework- motivated empirical study
authors: Xiao Hu & Jeremy T. D. Ng & Samuel K. W. Chu
summary_haiku: This study proposes a learning analytics framework for assessing wiki-supported collaborative learning quality across contribution, participation, transactivity, and social dynamics. Using mixed methods with 440 secondary students and six teachers, regression analyses and interviews revealed that students' and teachers' use of Wikiglass, an LA-enabled group awareness tool, significantly predicted collaboration quality metrics at individual and group levels, particularly when viewing other groups' analytics.

title: Emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on Civic Issues
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Omer Keynan & Orly Shapira
summary_haiku: This study examined emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on controversial civic issues among nine undergraduate students. Using mixed methods—analyzing 23 discussion turns through follow-up interviews—researchers compared how participants labeled their own emotions with how peers recognized them. Findings revealed low correlation between composers' emotion labeling and others' recognition, lack of shared emotional vocabulary, and two key recognition strategies: attributing emotions based on perceived closeness/belonging to topics, and using iconized visual imagery. Despite poor alignment, participants successfully communicated emotionally through dialogic engagement.

title: The impact of scripts on blended and online socially shared regulation of learning: A role‑playing game theory perspective
authors: Clyde A. Warden & Chi-Cheng Chang & James O. Stanworth & Judy F. Chen
summary_haiku: Researchers examined how brief "mere exposure prompts" (MEP) affect collaborative learning in role-playing game simulations across online and blended course formats. Using behavioral trace data and social network analysis with 185 students completing business negotiation tasks, they found MEP scripts significantly influenced planning behaviors in fully online learners but not blended learners, despite both groups recalling the prompt message. Results suggest online environments enable script-based interventions more effectively than traditional classroom settings.

title: Mediating and perspective‑taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective‑taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role‑play and reflection for microteaching
authors: Toshio Mochizuki & Hiroshi Sasaki & Takehiro Wakimoto & Yoshihiko Kubota & Brendan Eagan & Ryoya Hirayama & Yuta Yamaguchi & Natsumi Yuki & Hideo Funaoi & Hideyuki Suzuki & Hiroshi Kato
summary_haiku: This study examined how tangible puppets and 3D manipulable animations support student teachers' perspective-taking in microteaching. Using epistemic network analysis on discourse from 72 preservice teachers across three sessions, results showed that combining mediating manipulatives (puppets) with perspective-taking manipulatives (3D viewpoint switching) significantly enhanced student-centered reflection compared to video-only conditions. The intervention fostered authentic imaginary student voices and sustained dialogic teaching perspectives in subsequent role-plays.

title: Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low‑achieving students in knowledge building
authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: Low-achieving secondary students engaged in Knowledge Building through Knowledge Forum exhibited predominantly positive emotions, with joy comprising 53% of expressed emotions. Sequential pattern analysis revealed emotions tend to transition to similar emotions, and five primary emotional evolution paths emerged, with confusion serving as a critical juncture determining whether students progress toward joy or negative emotions like boredom and frustration.

title: Visions of the good in
authors: Etan Cohen & Dani Ben-Zvi & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This article examines ethical dimensions of design-based research in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a Knowledge Building Community case study, the authors propose three ethical frameworks—aretaic, deontological, and consequentialist—to help CSCL researchers systematically articulate their ideological commitments and visions of the good. They present a seven-question framework for unpacking these ethical foundations across design phases and demonstrate how empirical findings can refine moral principles iteratively.

title: An automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach to promoting collaborative knowledge building, group performance, and socially shared regulation in CSCL
authors: Lanqin Zheng & Miaolang Long & Jiayu Niu & Lu Zhong
summary_haiku: This study examined an automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach using deep neural networks in computer-supported collaborative learning. A quasi-experimental design with 120 college students in 40 groups compared the proposed approach to traditional online collaboration. Results showed significant improvements in cognitive, metacognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement; collaborative knowledge building; group performance; and socially shared regulation, without increasing cognitive load.

title: The temporal dynamics of online problem‑based learning: Why and when sequence matters
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
summary_haiku: This study analyzed 8,009 qualitatively coded interactions from 204 medical students across four online problem-based learning courses using sequence and process mining. Findings revealed that interaction sequences and their temporal order predicted student achievement better than interaction frequency alone. High-cognitive interactions (argumentation, evaluation) triggered similar high-level responses, while low-cognitive interactions perpetuated low-level engagement. Initiating interactions, regardless of cognitive content, showed strongest association with performance, highlighting the importance of sequential dynamics over simple participation counts.

title: An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-layered AI-driven analytical framework integrating learning analytics to examine collaborative problem-solving from a complex adaptive systems perspective. Analyzing multimodal data from 24 online group sessions using optimal matching, clustering, and hidden Markov modeling, researchers identified three distinct collaborative patterns: behavior-oriented (medium performance), communication-behavior-synergistic (high performance), and communication-oriented (low performance), revealing the multimodal, dynamic, and synergistic nature of group collaboration.

title: Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding
authors: Leonardo Silva & Antonio Mendes & Anabela Gomes & Gabriel Fortes
summary_haiku: # Summary This randomized controlled trial evaluated RESPE, a computer-supported collaborative learning platform embedding computational scaffolding for self-regulation and socially shared regulation of learning in introductory programming. With 71 students across three conditions (self-regulation support only, combined self and social regulation support, and control), results showed regulatory support significantly improved course grades. Notably, only students receiving social regulation support achieved superior collaborative activity performance, confirming the importance of social-cognitive perspectives in learning regulation.

title: Facilitated model‑based reasoning in immersive virtual reality: Meaning‑making and embodied interactions with dynamic processes
authors: Michelle Lui & Kit-Ying Angela Chong & Martha Mullally & Rhonda McEwen
summary_haiku: This study examined how 34 undergraduate students engaged with a lac operon VR simulation using head-mounted displays while a facilitator viewed a mirrored display. Using the Structure-Behavior-Function framework to code facilitator-participant interactions, researchers identified four patterns supporting model-based reasoning: spontaneous structural observations, immediate situated feedback, multiple simulated states comparison, and inquiry spanning structural-behavioral-functional levels. Findings demonstrate that facilitated VR simulations effectively support abstract scientific concept understanding through embodied interaction and dialogue.

title: Gesture‑mediated collaboration with augmented reality headsets in a problem‑based astronomy task
authors: James Planey & Robin Jephthah Rajarathinam & Emma Mercier & Robb Lindgren
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined 15 undergraduate groups collaborating on an astronomy problem using augmented reality headsets and tablets. Analysis revealed that gesture—particularly spatial pointing and representational gestures—mediated collaborative knowledge construction, especially during complex tasks. Groups with higher AR experience showed greater engagement. Gesture facilitated five key affordances: exploration, orientation, perspective-sharing, synthesizing representations, and symbolic conception. The findings demonstrate how embodied gesture bridges digital and physical spaces, enabling groups to create shared situated conceptual spaces that enhance collaborative problem-solving in extended reality environments.

title: Common “place” observations about embodiment and CSCL
authors: Victor R. Lee
summary_haiku: This commentary examines embodied computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) by arguing that shared physical or digital "place" is central to how multiple bodies coordinate learning. Unlike earlier embodied learning research focusing on individual sensorimotor experience, embodied CSCL leverages three key resources: differing relative perspectives, body motion/gesture, and common referents. The author proposes that foregrounding place in future embodied CSCL research and design could advance understanding of how technology mediates collaborative meaning-making among co-located learners.

title: Fostering collaborative and embodied learning
authors: Jacob Fortman & Rebecca Quintana
summary_haiku: Extended reality (XR) environments—including augmented, virtual, and mixed reality—offer significant potential for collaborative and embodied learning by enabling learners to use body-based resources for meaning-making. This special issue examines empirical research demonstrating how XR technologies support collaborative embodied learning across diverse contexts, from family geoscience exploration to teacher mathematics reasoning, addressing the gap between XR adoption in education and research grounded in collaborative learning theory.

title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
authors: Wen Huang & Candace Walkington & Mitchell J. Nathan
summary_haiku: This study examines how in-service teachers collaboratively construct geometric knowledge in shared VR environments using a novel multimodal analysis method. Analyzing 108 episodes across three groups, researchers identified strong simultaneous relationships between actions on virtual objects and collaborative speech, plus five emergent interaction themes. Results demonstrate that virtual objects effectively mediate collaborative knowledge-building, with structured activity design and moderate avatar realism supporting equitable, adaptable learning.

title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
authors: Xintian Tu & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Mengxi Zhou & Nitasha Mathayas & Noel Enyedy
summary_haiku: This study examines how first and second graders use embodied communication—gestures and body movements—within a mixed-reality environment to learn about particle states of matter. Using interaction analysis and coding schemes, researchers found students developed shared gestures representing challenging concepts during classroom activities and subsequently used these gestures in interviews to clarify understanding. Results reveal embodied communication serves both individual and collective functions, supporting collaborative knowledge construction about microscopic particle behavior and macroscopic state changes.

title: Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning‑on‑the‑move for place‑based geoscience sense‑making
authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land & Lillyanna Faimon & Yu-Chen Chiu
summary_haiku: This study investigated how families experienced immersion while using a mobile augmented reality app called Time Explorers to collaboratively learn about geologic time and geoscience processes during outdoor learning-on-the-move. Using interaction analysis of video recordings and interviews from 17 families (51 participants), researchers found that sensory and social immersion supported sense-making conversations and observational inquiry, while narrative and actional immersion enabled deep engagement with geoscience content about rock-water interactions shaping Appalachia.

title: The mechanism and effect of class-wide peer feedback on conceptual knowledge improvement: Does different feedback type matter?
authors: Jesmine S. H. Tan & Wenli Chen & Junzhu Su & Guo Su
summary_haiku: Class-wide peer feedback in computer-supported collaborative learning significantly improved students' conceptual knowledge about biological adaptations. Using mixed methods with 38 sixth-graders, researchers found that feedback seeking clarity and providing suggestions yielded highest response rates and knowledge improvement. Elaborated comments with moderate depth were most effective, while excessive elaboration proved cognitively demanding. Results demonstrate that intergroup peer feedback supports knowledge advancement when group-level cognitive capacity is maximized.

title: Does matching peers at finer‑grained levels of prior performance enhance gains in task performance from peer review?
authors: Zheng Zong & Christian D. Schunn
summary_haiku: This study examined whether matching peer reviewers and authors by four performance levels (rather than binary high/low) enhances task performance gains in online peer feedback. Using regression analysis on 766 biology students across multiple assignments, results revealed that providing feedback to same-level peers benefits reviewers, while receiving feedback shows mixed effects. Simulations indicated that performance-based matching algorithms produce better cumulative outcomes than random assignment across all student performance levels.

title: Promoting knowledge building through meta‑discourse and epistemic discourse understanding
authors: Yuyao Tong & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: # Summary This quasi-experimental study examined how meta-discourse—students' reflection on and inquiry into their collaborative discourse—promotes epistemic discourse understanding and productive knowledge-building inquiry. Ninth-grade visual arts students (n=63) in two classes used Knowledge Forum for online collaboration. The experimental class engaged in classroom meta-discourse reflecting on discourse processes, principles, and idea development, while the comparison class used regular discussion. Results showed experimental students developed deeper epistemic discourse understanding and domain knowledge, engaged in more sophisticated knowledge-building discourse moves, and demonstrated stronger relationships between epistemic understanding and productive inquiry, suggesting meta-discourse effectively supports collaborative learning.

title: Exploring the impact of chat‑based collaborative activities and SRL‑focused interventions on students’ self‑regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs
authors: Georgios Psathas & Stergios Tegos & Stavros N. Demetriadis & Thrasyvoulos Tsiatsos
summary_haiku: This study examined how self-regulated learning (SRL) interventions combined with chat-based collaborative activities affect MOOC students' outcomes. Using a programming MOOC with 1,807 participants, researchers compared control, general intervention, and personalized intervention groups. Results showed personalized interventions significantly improved SRL profiles and course retention (87.5% vs. 62.5%), while both intervention types increased collaborative participation and learning outcomes compared to controls, demonstrating that targeted SRL support enhances engagement and completion in MOOCs.

title: Identifying collaborative problem‑solver profiles based on collaborative processing time, actions and skills on a computer‑based task
authors: Yue Ma & Huilin Zhang & Li Ni & Da Zhou
summary_haiku: This study employed latent profile analysis on PISA 2015 data from 1,677 Chinese students to identify four distinct collaborative problem-solver profiles based on time-on-task, actions-on-task, and three CPS skills: Disengaged, Struggling, Adaptive, and Excellent. Results revealed that gender, socioeconomic status, and attitudes toward collaboration significantly predicted profile membership, while achievement motivation did not. Profile membership correlated with CPS performance differences.

title: Understanding the effect of differences in prior knowledge on middle school students’ collaborative interactions and learning
authors: Sadhana Puntambekar & Dana Gnesdilow & Sinan Yavuz
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how prior knowledge variance within collaborative groups affects middle school students' science learning and interactions. Using hierarchical linear modeling on 102 groups and social network analysis of two contrasting groups, researchers found that students in homogeneous groups achieved significantly greater learning gains than those in heterogeneous groups. Qualitative analysis revealed homogeneous groups exhibited more distributed, reciprocal interactions with mutual scaffolding, while heterogeneous groups showed centralized interactions dominated by the highest-knowledge member, resulting in lower engagement and learning for less-knowledgeable peers.

title: Can CPS better prepare 8th graders for problem‑solving in electromagnetism and bridging the gap between high‑ and low‑achievers than IPS?
authors: Jiun-Wei Guo & Hsiao-Ching She & Meng-Jun Chen & Pei-Yi Tsai
summary_haiku: This study compared collaborative problem-solving (CPS) and individual problem-solving (IPS) approaches in an online electromagnetism unit with 109 eighth graders. Using simulation-based instruction across five classes, researchers found CPS significantly enhanced problem-solving performance compared to IPS, while both equally improved conceptual understanding. Critically, CPS more effectively boosted low-achievers' performance and narrowed achievement gaps, as low-achievers received greater peer support during collaboration.

title: The role of first‑language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self‑efficacy in CSCL
authors: Natalia Reich-Stiebert & Jennifer Raimann & Stefan Sturmer
summary_haiku: Students in linguistically heterogeneous CSCL groups exhibited lower gains in online interaction self-efficacy than those in homogeneous groups, regardless of their own language status. This nine-week pretest-posttest study of 1,525 distance education students found that task-related communication during initial collaboration moderated this negative effect, while social bonding activities paradoxically amplified perceived heterogeneity and impaired self-efficacy development.

title: Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning
authors: Reet Kasepalu & Pankaj Chejara & Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley
summary_haiku: This quasi-experiment examined how dashboards affect teacher withitness—situational awareness and interventions—during collaborative learning. Twenty-four teachers used three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring-only dashboard, and AI-assisted alerting & guiding dashboard. Results show mirroring dashboards increased situational awareness, while alerting & guiding dashboards significantly reduced teacher workload, particularly frustration and perceived failure. However, intervention rates didn't increase as hypothesized, suggesting teachers need extended training to effectively implement AI-suggested coregulation strategies in authentic classroom settings.

title: Co‑constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective
authors: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle
summary_haiku: # Summary Cress and Kimmerle examine how generative AI tools like ChatGPT can support human knowledge construction from a computer-supported collaborative learning perspective. While AI lacks conceptual understanding, they argue that appropriate prompts enabling argumentative dialogue between humans and AI can facilitate knowledge transformation beyond simple information exchange. The authors propose future CSCL research directions including ethnomethodological studies, experimental investigations of prompting strategies, and exploration of whether genuine collaborative knowledge construction occurs between human-AI dyads.

title: Taking a stance in the process of learning: Developing perspectival understandings through knowledge co‑construction during synchronous computer‑mediated classroom discussion
authors: Hannah Park & Diane L. Schallert & Kyle M. Williams & Rachel E. Gaines & Jeonghyun Lee & van de Sande
summary_haiku: This study examined how graduate students expressed perspectives through stancetaking during synchronous online classroom discussions. Using Du Bois' discourse framework, researchers analyzed 27 chat transcripts, coding for epistemic, affective, and evaluative stances alongside positioning, evaluation, and alignment acts. Findings revealed students predominantly adopted epistemic stances focused on knowledge acquisition, with shifts in discussion topics marking moments of perspectival understanding development. The analysis demonstrates how collaborative knowledge co-construction occurs through iterative combinations of subsidiary stance acts.

title: Effects of group awareness support in CSCL on students’ learning performance: A three‑level meta‑analysis
authors: Dengkang Chen & Yi Zhang & Heng Luo & Zhifang Zhu & Jingsi Ma & Yuru Lin
summary_haiku: Group awareness support in computer-supported collaborative learning shows moderate positive effects on student learning performance (g = 0.46). A three-level meta-analysis of 46 studies found greatest impact on cognitive development, followed by behavioral participation and social emotion. Combined awareness types outperformed individual types, and larger groups benefited more than smaller groups from awareness support.

title: Exploring students’ immersive VR experiences as resources for collaborative meaning making and learning
authors: Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier & Hans Christian Arnseth
summary_haiku: Students viewing a cinematic VR film about exclusion and discrimination, followed by teacher-facilitated group dialogues, experienced the VR as highly social. Through interaction analysis of reflective dialogues, researchers identified four dimensions characterizing meaning-making: feeling part of conversations, attending to others' bodily expressions, students' own bodily responses, and teacher guidance. The study demonstrates how immersive VR experiences become collaborative learning resources when integrated into structured activity sequences emphasizing dialogue.

title: Learning within fiber‑crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human‑material collaboration
authors: Anna Keune
summary_haiku: This study employs posthumanist analysis to examine how middle school students and fiber craft materials collaboratively produce algorithms during weaving and fabric manipulation activities. Using video data, the researcher identifies how youth-material intra-actions create computational performances through repeated, patterned movements. Findings reveal that both humans and materials actively contribute to algorithmic production, with variations in these patterns enabling algorithmic expansion over time. The study proposes human-material collaboration as a productive analytical unit for understanding computational learning in CSCL contexts.

title: Reflective assessment using analytics and artifacts for scaffolding knowledge building competencies among undergraduate students
authors: Yuqin Yang & Carol K. K. Chan & Gaoxia Zhu & Yuyao Tong & Daner Sun
summary_haiku: # Summary This study develops a comprehensive framework of knowledge building (KB) competencies encompassing conceptual, metacognitive, socio-emotional, and epistemic dimensions. Using qualitative discourse analysis of 1,390 Knowledge Forum notes from 41 undergraduates, the research demonstrates that reflective assessment enriched with super synthesis notes, KB interaction rubrics, and KBDeX learning analytics visualizations significantly fosters development of these competencies. Results show undergraduates engaged in higher-level productive discourse moves across all dimensions, with sequential pattern analysis revealing progressive improvements in socio-emotional interactions and epistemic engagement between pre- and post-intervention stages.

title: Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Rotem Abdu
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how professional development affects mathematics teachers' ability to notice dialogue in computer-supported collaborative learning. Fourteen teachers analyzed video excerpts of student pairs solving parabola tasks before and after an 80-minute intervention focused on Bakhtinian dialogic concepts. Using think-aloud interviews and dialogic framework analysis, results showed significant improvements in teachers' attending to and responding to dialogic attributes, particularly regarding student relationships, inter-animation, and multivoicedness, though challenges remain in balancing mathematical correctness with dialogue support.

title: Dialogues across time and space in a video‑based collaborative learning environment
authors: Charlotte Beal & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examines how pre-service teachers' dialogues emerged across time and space as they collaboratively constructed video-based mind maps using a Padlet platform. Through interaction analysis of 28 hours of video recordings, the researchers found that video-based mind maps supported multiple space-time constellations—synchronous small-group conversations, asynchronous group-to-group exchanges, and whole-class dialogues—enabling meaning-making across learning levels. The study demonstrates how shared video dialogues functioned as mediational artifacts connecting individual contributions into networked conversations that supported collaborative learning and exam preparation.

title: Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement
authors: Lisa Paneth & Loris T. Jeitziner & Oliver Rack & Klaus Opwis & Carmen Zahn
summary_haiku: This study examined how nonverbal behaviors relate to collaborative group engagement quality in computer-supported learning. Using video analysis of 38 university groups completing a design task, researchers applied quantitative mixed-effects models to 2,617 one-minute sequences and qualitative case analysis. Findings revealed that nodding, eye contact, and gesturing positively correlate with social, cognitive, and conceptual engagement, while laughing shows complex relationships across dimensions. The research demonstrates nonverbal behaviors serve as meaningful indicators of multifaceted, dynamic group engagement in collaborative learning contexts.

title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
authors: Sini Davies & Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen
summary_haiku: Student teams engaged in open-ended collaborative invention projects applied maker practices—design, computer engineering, product design, and science—in iterative, nonlinear processes. Video analysis of three seventh-grade teams revealed that embodied practices like sketching and material experimentation were essential for advancing shared epistemic objects. Teacher scaffolding and peer tutoring effectively supported knowledge creation, though excessive direction could oversimplify designs and reduce engagement.

title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
authors: Bo Yang
summary_haiku: This study examines how danmaku and discussion boards accommodate mass participation in MOOCs through mixed-method analysis of 2,435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion board posts. Findings reveal danmaku fosters collective indirect interaction emphasizing socio-emotional dimensions, while discussion boards organize learners into threaded small groups supporting direct cognitive discussions. The complementary tools enable scalable, sociable collaborative learning environments addressing both emotional and knowledge-sharing needs.

title: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This study tested the Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model using structural equation modeling across three medical education studies (N=504). Analyzing simulation-based diagnostic tasks, researchers found that content and collaboration knowledge influenced collaborative diagnostic activities (evidence elicitation and sharing), which subsequently affected diagnostic accuracy, justification, and efficiency. Notably, collaboration knowledge emerged as more critical than social skills, and diagnostic activities independently predicted outcomes beyond individual characteristics, highlighting the multidimensional nature of collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains.

title: The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
authors: Andrew Zamecnik & Georg Grossmann & Djazia Ladjal & Abelardo Pardo
summary_haiku: # Summary This mixed-methods study examined task cohesion development in 194 collaborative learning teams using temporal network motif analysis combined with survey data. Teams were classified into four transition groups based on cohesion perception changes across a three-week work-integrated learning program. Findings revealed that teams maintaining aligned perceptions demonstrated higher performance and greater triadic interaction patterns, while teams with divergent perceptions showed lower performance and dyadic interactions. Temporal network motifs proved effective as proxies for task cohesion, validating the approach for understanding team dynamics in collaborative learning environments.

title: Comparing the effectiveness of CSCL scripts for shared task perceptions in socially shared regulation of collaborative learning
authors: Mariel Miller & Allyson F. Hadwin
summary_haiku: High-support group planning scripts significantly improved undergraduate students' accuracy of shared task perceptions and transactive planning discussions compared to low-support scripts, though individual-level support showed no detectable effect. However, enhanced task perceptions did not translate to improved group performance, suggesting groups may struggle to implement shared understanding during task execution.

title: Students’ use of technological tools to engage in collective mathematical proof activity
authors: Tenchita Alzaga Elizondo & David Brown
summary_haiku: Using instrumental genesis theory, this study examined how students in a remote introduction to proofs course operationalized Google Docs and Zoom to engage in collaborative proof activity. Analysis of six episodes revealed students developed collective utilization schemes coordinating visual mediators with verbal communication to enable collective argumentation and co-construct solutions through iterative text refinement. Google Docs' simultaneous editing and referencing features particularly supported active, process-oriented proof writing.

title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher‑order thinking
authors: M. Borge & B. K. Smith & T. Aldemir
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examines whether generative AI can support higher-order thinking through human-computer collaboration. An expert in collaborative learning engaged in extended dialogue with ChatGPT, practicing metacognitive and sociometacognitive skills while reflecting on interaction quality using a framework of six communication patterns. Findings indicate ChatGPT feasibly supports both individual metacognition and collective sensemaking when users actively regulate conversations and employ structured reflection prompts, though limitations like tendency toward definitive unsupported claims require human oversight for effective learning.

title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
authors: Anders I. Mørch & Renate Andersen & Siv Eie & Louise Mifsud
summary_haiku: This study investigates how shared understanding emerges in computer-mediated learning using Minecraft for social studies. Through design-based research with student teachers reconstructing historical industrial sites, researchers identified "emergent group understanding"—a phenomenon where spontaneous individual knowledge contributions trigger focused group action toward shared learning goals. The framework integrates sociotechnical congruence, intersubjectivity, and emergence theories, revealing how social and technological objects co-evolve through six states of intersubjectivity toward knowledge objects.

title: Contesting sociocomputational norms: Computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
summary_haiku: This interaction analysis study examines how elementary and middle school students and instructors negotiate refactoring—revising working code—in a programming workshop. Using stancetaking, sociocomputational norms, and inequity frameworks, researchers analyzed 20 minutes of classroom discourse. Findings reveal that while students initially debated coding approaches, instructors progressively endorsed loops as superior, amplifying relational inequity by devaluing alternative strategies and limiting discussion of efficiency's multiple interpretations.

title: Revealing the interplay of cognitive, meta‑cognitive, and social processes in university students’ collaborative problem solving: a three‑stage analytical framework
authors: Shuowen An & Si Zhang & Zhihui Cai & Wei Pan & Mingwei Li & Mingwen Tong
summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-stage analytical framework to examine collaborative problem-solving (CPS) patterns among 24 university students completing instructional design and multimedia development tasks. Using dynamic time warping for clustering and process mining analysis, the researchers identified two distinct CPS subgroups: solution-driven groups that effectively transitioned from divergent to convergent thinking through meta-cognitive monitoring, and problem-driven groups that focused on task requirements but lacked comprehensive evaluation processes, resulting in lower performance outcomes.

title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
authors: Ramy Elmoazen & Mohammed Saqr & Laura Hirsto & Matti Tedre
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study analyzed 135 dental students' online problem-based learning discussions across four courses using Community of Inquiry framework coding combined with latent class analysis, epistemic network analysis, and process mining. Three distinct roles emerged: leaders, social mediators, and peripheral explorers. Students exhibited stable role trajectories across time, with active trajectories achieving higher grades than free riders, suggesting roles function as stable dispositions requiring intentional teacher intervention for change.

title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
authors: Sebastian Strauss & Isis Tunnigkeit & Julia Eberle & Arlind Avdullahu & Nikol Rummel
doi: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared external collaboration scripts and reflection scaffolds for fostering collaboration skills in 150 university students working in groups. Using multilevel modeling, researchers found that learners receiving collaborative reflection gained significantly more knowledge about effective collaboration than those using scripts or no support. However, neither intervention improved subsequent interaction quality. Results suggest reflection-based approaches may offer autonomy-supportive alternatives to directive scripting for knowledge acquisition.

title: Correction: Contesting sociocomputational norms: computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
summary_haiku: This correction clarifies a discrepancy in the theoretical framework section of an interaction analysis study examining how computer programming instructors and students contest sociocomputational norms through classroom discourse. The researchers use stancetaking analysis to investigate participatory and relational inequities without assuming participants' inner experiences, focusing on how meanings are publicly negotiated.

title: Correction: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a structural equation modeling study examining collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains. The original article contained a sign error in Table 5, where most coefficients were incorrectly prefixed with negative signs. The corrected version has been published online.

title: How do new ideas come to be adopted during discourse?
authors: Deanna Kuhn & Teresa Fraguada & Mariel Halpern
summary_haiku: This study examines how adolescents adopt and revise ideas during electronic peer argumentation. Two case studies traced participants' evolving positions across eight successive dialogs on juvenile justice. Results revealed contrasting patterns: one participant readily adopted partners' ideas but struggled defending positions, while the other maintained firm beliefs with strong counterargument skills but limited openness to new ideas. Findings highlight how argumentation skills, epistemological understanding, and metacognitive reflection jointly influence belief change in collaborative discourse.

title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group‑level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
authors: Kateryna Zabolotna & Liv Nøhr & Megumi Iwata & Daniel Spikol & Jonna Malmberg & Hanna Jarvenoja
summary_haiku: Task design significantly shapes collaborative learning processes. This study compared a conceptual physics drawing task and a hands-on robotics task involving secondary students, analyzing collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation using video coding and network analysis. Conceptually oriented tasks promoted prolonged cognitive engagement and stronger connections between cognitive regulation and negotiation, while hands-on tasks featured frequent but brief knowledge construction episodes emphasizing socioemotional interactions for maintaining collaboration.

title: Toward multimodal learning analytics in simulation‑based collaborative learning: A design ethnography of maritime training
authors: Charlott Sellberg & Amit Sharma
summary_haiku: # Summary This design ethnography examines maritime simulator-based training to inform multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) development. Through detailed video analysis of master mariner students' collaborative bridge activities, the researchers identified how instructors deliver embedded assessments and feedback using multiple social and material resources. The study proposes specific technologies—system logs, eye-tracking, and speech recognition—necessary for capturing professional performance, communication, and collaboration in simulation-based learning environments.

title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
authors: Jinzhi Zhou & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Zach Ryan & Christina Stiso & Danielle Murphy & Joshua Danish & Clark A. Chinn & Ravit Golan Duncan
summary_haiku: Fifth-grade students engaged in peer critique within a computer-supported collaborative learning environment predominantly used soft disagreements (64%) rather than direct forms when critiquing groupmates' scientific models. Using conversation analysis, researchers found that students effectively resolved disagreements consensually in 88.6% of episodes, advancing collective knowledge through both direct and soft disagreement forms, while maintaining positive group dynamics.

title: Correction to: Many are the ways to learn: Identifying multi‑modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno & Pierre Dillenbourg
summary_haiku: This correction document addresses formatting and citation errors in the original 2021 article examining multi-modal behavioral profiles in collaborative constructivist learning. The researchers identified and corrected a missing colon in the title and multiple misattributed or incorrectly formatted citations throughout the paper, ensuring accurate reference to their prior work on collaborative learning analytics.

title: Correction: An artificial intelligence‑driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem‑solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for an article on artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics examining collaborative problem-solving through complex adaptive systems theory. The correction addresses an erroneous figure that appeared in the original publication, replacing it with the correct framework diagram of complex adaptive systems theory adapted from Holland's work.

title: Collaborative science? Formalism and a unified language: Future directions for computer‑supported collaborative learning
authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Hans C. Arnseth & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: # Summary This article responds to calls for unified language and formalism in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). Rather than endorsing computational modeling approaches, the authors propose a meta-stance centered on learning mechanisms that integrate cognitive, socio-cognitive, and sociocultural perspectives. They advocate for analyzing moment-by-moment meaning-making through dialogue, mediational tools, and meaning potentials, arguing this approach better captures collaborative learning processes than probabilistic models alone. The authors present an exchange structure formalism and emphasize mechanistic causality in qualitative research to build cumulative CSCL knowledge.

title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
authors: Pengjin Wang & Fan Chen & Deliang Wang & Gaowei Chen
summary_haiku: Visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) using classroom discourse analysis enhanced primary students' collaborative learning. A 3-month intervention with 53 students showed significant knowledge gains in the high-dose group and increased student participation across both groups. Qualitative analysis revealed students engaged in deeper reflection on problem-solving strategies, group collaboration, and whole-class participation when reviewing visualised classroom discourse through discussion forums.

title: Activity‑based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
authors: Lucas Paulsen & Jacob Davidsen
summary_haiku: Paulsen and Davidsen propose Activity-Based Collaborative Virtual Reality (ABC-VR), a conceptual framework grounded in activity theory for designing and researching collaborative learning in immersive 360-degree video environments. Unlike existing individual-focused concepts, ABC-VR emphasizes social knowledge construction through analyzing recorded real-world activities at multiple levels—examining what actions occur, how they're performed, and why. The framework positions learners collaboratively engaging with situated practices from educational, social, and work contexts.

title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self‑assessment scale (QCGE‑SAS)
authors: Loris T. Jeitziner & Lisa Paneth & Oliver Rack & Susanne Bleisch & Carmen Zahn
summary_haiku: This study developed and validated the QCGE-SAS, a 13-item self-assessment scale measuring quality of collaborative group engagement across four dimensions: behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential engagement. Using confirmatory factor analysis with 246 higher education students, the scale demonstrated good model fit and construct validity through correlations with related measures. Three subscales showed acceptable reliability; however, the social engagement subscale exhibited suboptimal internal consistency, warranting future refinement.

title: Understanding the role of I‑positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer‑supported collaborative learning environment
authors: Aaron J. Peltoniemi & Joni Lamsa & Sami Lehesvuori
summary_haiku: This qualitative study applies discourse analysis and dialogical self theory to investigate how interpersonal and intrapersonal voices facilitate knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning. Analyzing ten physics students in two groups, researchers identified discourse functions and I-positions (I–it, I–me, I–you, I–we) within dialogues. The successful group employed both interpersonal and intrapersonal voices, with intrapersonal voices peaking during empirical evaluation, while the unsuccessful group relied predominantly on interpersonal voices focused on individual-level concerns rather than collective elaboration.

title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
authors: Shihui Feng & Ziyi Wei
summary_haiku: This systematic review of 66 studies (2005-2024) proposes the CoMPAS framework for modeling individual participation in collaborative learning using process data. The framework identifies six forms of participation—cognitive interactions, coordinative interactions, metacognitive interactions, passive participation, solo active participation, and socio-emotional interactions—analyzed through oral conversational, textual, log, and nonverbal physical data using descriptive, content, network, and clustering methods. Findings reveal bidirectional relationships between individual participation and group performance.

title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
authors: Alena Seredko
summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how software developers collaboratively frame programming problems on Stack Overflow through asynchronous, fluid participation. Using trace ethnography and sequential analysis of selected threads, the research reveals that minimal reproducible examples (MREs) structured within the platform's dual-space design enable collaboration at scale. Standardized norm-enforcing requests and explicit referencing practices ensure mutual intelligibility among unknown contributors, facilitating effective problem-solving in large-scale online environments.

title: Age‑related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
authors: Shigen Shimojo & Yugo Hayashi
summary_haiku: Younger adults demonstrated significantly higher learning performance and concept map quality than older adults during collaborative learning with concept maps using attribution theory. While younger adults engaged more frequently in active utterances and showed stronger connections between constructive and interactive behaviors, older adults exhibited higher constructive and interactive utterance frequencies but stronger active-interactive connections. Epistemic network analysis revealed that older adults required knowledge reactivation during elaboration, suggesting age-related cognitive decline hinders knowledge integration in computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
authors: Changhao Liang & Yuko Toyokawa & Hiroaki Ogata
summary_haiku: A mixed genetic algorithm embedded in a learning platform optimizes group formation for EFL active reading by balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous student characteristics using marker data. Implemented in a Japanese high school classroom with 39 students, the system significantly improved vocabulary learning gains and demonstrated positive group dynamics through Wordcloud visualization, with 85% of students reporting the tool's helpfulness for collaborative tasks.

title: Collaboration in virtual and remote laboratories for education: A systematic literature review
authors: Azzeddine Benabbou & Catherine Pons
summary_haiku: This systematic literature review examined 62 educational virtual and remote laboratories published 2011-2025 to assess collaboration support. While communication and group awareness tools are well-integrated, guidance and regulation tools remain underrepresented. Most laboratories support synchronous, non-co-located collaboration in STEM disciplines. Evaluation studies show predominantly positive learning outcomes, yet only one-third assess collaboration quality, indicating a significant research gap requiring future investigation.
